topic: "In 90% of runs" is not "a 90% promise": how to read a simulation honestly

assumptions.notes: Eva: €50,000 invested plus €1,000 a month for 30 years, simulated 10,000 times by scripts/simulate-projection-paths.mjs (seed 43): yearly real equity returns resampled independently from an equal-weighted portfolio of up to 16 developed markets, 1900 to 2020 (Jordà-Schularick-Taylor Macrohistory Database R6), shifted to a 6% arithmetic mean. 10th percentile €511,818 (shown as €510k), median €1,076,959, 90th €2,212,833. So 90% of runs ended above about €510,000. Illustrative.

columnStory.disclosure: Illustrative. 10,000 runs on past yearly returns, set to a 6% average.

hookVariants.narration: A simulation says ninety percent. It is not saying what you think.
Your retirement calculator says ninety percent. Here is what that number actually means.

beats.narration: Eva ran her plan ten thousand times, each year drawn from real market history. In ninety percent of runs, her pot passed about five hundred and ten thousand.
That is the honest sentence. In ninety percent of runs, under these assumptions.
It is not a promise about Eva. It holds only under the model's assumptions, and her job and health are not in the model.
So keep the assumptions attached to the number.
Read as a promise about you, the same number claims more than the model can.
So read any simulation this way. Say in ninety percent of runs. Then ask whether you could live on the bad luck run. Future returns are not guaranteed.

rows.label: Could I live on the bad luck run?

cta.narration: Save this for the next time a calculator gives you a percentage.

caption.instagram:
A simulation says 90%. It is not saying what you think.

Eva ran her plan 10,000 times, each year's return drawn from developed market history. In 90% of runs, her pot passed about €510,000 after 30 years. That is the model's estimate under its assumptions, not a promise that Eva will have it. The future can differ from the past, and her job and health are not in the model.

The honest reading: say "in 90% of runs" with the assumptions attached, look at the bad luck end, and ask whether you could live on it.
